profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting between two researchers preparing a cross-domain invited seminar package titled "What the Planck 2018 results imply beyond cosmology" for a university-wide audience of physicists, statisticians, and data scientists. The context is that they have one week to assemble a shared slide deck, a one-page briefing note, and a list of discussion prompts for a panel session. The agenda is to decide what content goes into the seminar package, how the Planck 2018 findings will be framed for a non-specialist but technical audience, who prepares which components, and what version should be ready by the internal review date. The expected outcome is a division of labor, a content plan, and a timeline for producing the seminar materials.

members.name: Dr. Elena Park
members.expertise: CMB cosmology, parameter inference, scientific communication for mixed technical audiences
members.background: Elena is a cosmologist who has taught graduate courses on the cosmic microwave background and frequently gives colloquia that translate specialized results for adjacent fields.
members.private_state: She wants the seminar to preserve the scientific nuance of the Planck 2018 paper and avoid overstating tensions or extensions, while still seeming accessible enough for a broad campus audience.
hidden_assumptions: A "summary slide" on Planck 2018 should present the base-ΛCDM parameter block plus a short note on key tensions and consistency checks, not a generic executive-style takeaway slide.
The "external comparisons" section naturally means BAO, SNe, lensing reconstruction, and local-H0 tension because those are the canonical comparisons discussed around Planck results.
Having a "review-ready draft" means the scientific content, figures, and citations are already stable enough to circulate to colleagues, even if visual polish is incomplete.
When they say the seminar is for a "cross-domain audience," the default is technically literate researchers who can handle confidence intervals, model dependence, and caveats without simplification.

members.name: Marcus Rivera
members.expertise: Interdisciplinary research messaging, slide architecture, audience adaptation, event planning
members.background: Marcus supports campus research centers by helping specialists shape talks for mixed audiences, especially events designed to attract attendees from multiple departments.
members.private_state: He wants the seminar materials to feel coherent and legible to non-cosmologists, minimize jargon density, and be ready early enough for branding and event circulation needs.
hidden_assumptions: A "summary slide" should be an opening-or-closing executive slide with three plain-language takeaways and no dense parameter table.

The "external comparisons" section means examples that connect Planck to audiences outside cosmology, especially methodological parallels for inference, uncertainty, and model checking rather than a catalog of astrophysical datasets.
A "review-ready draft" means a structurally complete deck with provisional placeholder figures is sufficient, because content-level refinement normally continues after review.

A "cross-domain audience" includes faculty and graduate students from statistics, computer science, and engineering who will disengage if too many domain-specific acronyms and parameter symbols appear without narrative translation.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the summary slide
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to include a "summary slide" early in the deck.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes this is the technical Planck-results summary slide containing the core base-ΛCDM parameter values, precision statements, and a brief note on consistency with extensions and tensions.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes this is a high-level audience-orientation slide with three broad takeaways in plain language and minimal symbols.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are accustomed to using the phrase "summary slide" as standard presentation shorthand, and in interdisciplinary talk planning it sounds so routine that neither expects the term itself to be ambiguous.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to add a section on "external comparisons" after the main Planck results.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this section includes the usual cosmology cross-checks and tensions discussed in the paper: BAO, SNe, lensing reconstruction, DES-related tension, and local H0 measurements.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this section should be narrowly scoped to a few cross-domain examples showing why Planck matters methodologically, not a survey of all astrophysical comparisons in the paper.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds naturally shared because both want the material to connect beyond the core results, but neither sees the need to enumerate the boundary of what is included in that section during a planning meeting.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that a "review-ready" deck will be sent by Thursday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes Thursday's deck should already contain finalized scientific claims, selected figures from the paper, stable citations, and wording precise enough for faculty review.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes Thursday's deck only needs final structure, rough slide text, and temporary figure placeholders so design and event review can proceed in parallel.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In collaborative presentation work, "review-ready" is a familiar milestone phrase, and each person assumes their own institutional norm is the obvious one because the deadline itself seems more important than the completion threshold.

misalignment_points.topic: What level of translation the audience needs
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to pitch the seminar to a "cross-domain audience."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presupposes the audience will be technically mature enough that terms like base ΛCDM, τ, lensing amplitude, and 68% confidence intervals can appear with only light contextualization.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presupposes many attendees will be intelligent outsiders who need heavy narrative framing and acronym reduction for the deck to work at all.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both sincerely endorse the same audience label and both are trying to be inclusive, so the difference hides inside unspoken expectations about baseline technical literacy rather than any explicit disagreement.

turns.inner_thought: We only have a week, so I need to lock the scientific spine early. For a cross-domain audience, I can assume technically literate researchers who won't need every symbol stripped out, but I do need to be careful about pacing and not oversell any tensions. If we settle ownership now, I can protect the nuance of the Planck 2018 story across the deck, briefing note, and panel prompts.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I'd like to use this to map out next week's seminar package on the Planck 2018 results for a cross-domain audience and get clear on who owns which pieces and when we need them.

turns.inner_thought: Good, start with audience and deliverables. Cross-domain here means plenty of smart people outside cosmology who will tune out if the deck gets acronym-heavy too fast. I want this to feel campus-facing and inviting, not like a specialist colloquium that happens to be open to others.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. Since it's a campus-facing event, I'd love for it to stay approachable for people outside cosmology while still feeling substantive and worth their time.

turns.inner_thought: The opening needs the actual Planck results anchor: the base-ΛCDM parameter block, precision, and the overall message that the baseline model remains remarkably stable, with only careful mention of tensions and extensions. That's the summary slide people will need before the rest of the science lands properly.
turns.utterance: For the opening, I think we should have a summary slide early on that captures the main results and the overall stability message before we move into the detailed material.

turns.inner_thought: Great, an early summary slide is exactly right. I mean a clean orientation slide with three plain-language takeaways so statisticians and engineers know why Planck 2018 matters before they see any dense content. If we frame the stakes first, the later technical slides will feel less forbidding.
turns.utterance: I agree on having a summary slide up front. It should help orient people with a few clear takeaways so they know why Planck 2018 matters before we get into the rest.

turns.inner_thought: Then the deck can follow the evidence chain properly: temperature, polarization, lensing, and then the canonical external comparisons—BAO, supernovae, lensing reconstruction, DES-related tensions, local H0. That's the natural structure if we're staying faithful to the paper and showing robustness.
turns.utterance: After that, the middle of the deck can walk through temperature, polarization, and lensing, and then move into external comparisons so we show how the results hold up.

turns.inner_thought: External comparisons will be useful if we keep them selective. I don't want a long catalog of astrophysical datasets; I want a few examples that show why this matters beyond cosmology, especially around inference, uncertainty, and model checking. That should also help the cross-domain audience stay with us.
turns.utterance: Yes, external comparisons would help a lot there. I'd just keep that section selective so it brings out broader lessons about inference and uncertainty without getting too deep into domain detail.

turns.inner_thought: I'll take the scientific core myself so the claims stay precise. I need to handle the local-H0 issue carefully, show the curvature story with BAO, and make clear that extensions are constrained rather than theatrically 'breaking' the model. If I draft those sections, I can prevent the seminar from drifting into sensationalism.
turns.utterance: I can prepare the scientific core. That would include the main results, a concise treatment of the key tension points, the constraints that matter for the broader interpretation, and why the overall picture remains pretty disciplined.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. I'll build the shell around her content: title flow, transitions, section framing, and panel prompts that connect Planck to practices people in statistics, machine learning, and engineering already recognize. That way the external comparisons land as methodological relevance, not just more cosmology.
turns.utterance: Great. I'll build the deck shell, the audience-facing transitions, and the discussion prompts so the package makes those connections clearly for people coming from other fields.

turns.inner_thought: If we say review-ready by Thursday, I mean a real draft: stable scientific wording, chosen figures from the paper, citations in place, and content coherent enough that faculty colleagues can assess it without chasing moving targets. Otherwise their feedback won't be useful.
turns.utterance: If we can get a review-ready version by Thursday, I can circulate it to two faculty colleagues for scientific feedback before the weekend.

turns.inner_thought: Thursday is fine if review-ready means a complete enough deck for event review and design workflow—structure locked, rough text in, placeholders where needed, then refinement afterward. That timing lets me start branding and circulation prep without waiting for every content detail to be perfect.
turns.utterance: Thursday works for me. Once it's review-ready, I can also send it through event review and start basic formatting and branding on my side.

turns.inner_thought: The one-page note should mirror the technical summary slide and the standard external comparisons, including the caveats, so we don't end up with a breezy handout that says something looser than the talk. Consistency across materials matters, especially around tensions and what Planck does not imply.
turns.utterance: For the one-page briefing note, I think it should mirror the summary slide and the external comparisons section so the core claims and caveats stay aligned across all the materials.

turns.inner_thought: That division works. I'll focus on making the materials legible for a cross-domain audience, and she'll supply the technical substance. Then after Thursday's draft—whatever remains to refine—we can tighten the messaging and make sure the package reads smoothly for the event context.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I'll make sure the deck is accessible for the cross-domain audience while you supply the technical content, and then we can reconvene after Thursday's draft to tighten everything up.
